title: No Way to Win Against God
overview: Job agrees that God is just in principle, but says no human could ever win a fair hearing against a God so powerful, and he wishes someone could stand between them.

parts.label: Who can win against God? (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Job grants his friend Bildad's point that God does not twist justice, then asks how any human could ever be proved right before God. He pictures a court case where God could raise a thousand questions or charges and a person could not answer even one.

parts.label: Power over all creation (vv. 5-13)
parts.note: Job describes God moving mountains, shaking the earth, darkening the sun, walking on the sea and setting the star groups in the sky, all without being seen. Rahab is a sea monster from ancient stories that stood for chaos, and even its helpers bow before God.

parts.label: No fair hearing possible (vv. 14-20)
parts.note: Even if Job were innocent, he says, he could only beg for mercy, because God is both stronger than him and the one who sets the rules of the court. He fears God would not even listen and that his own words would end up condemning him.

parts.label: Blameless and wicked alike (vv. 21-24)
parts.note: In his boldest lines, Job says God destroys the good and the wicked the same, ignores the suffering of the innocent, and blinds judges so injustice wins, then asks: if not God, who? This flatly challenges his friends' belief that suffering always proves guilt.

parts.label: Days slipping away (vv. 25-31)
parts.note: Job's life rushes past like a running messenger, a light reed boat or a diving eagle, with nothing good in it. However thoroughly he washed himself, he feels God would throw him back into the filth, so trying to clear his name seems pointless.

parts.label: Longing for a go-between (vv. 32-35)
parts.note: Because God is not a human Job can face as an equal, Job wishes for someone who could stand between them, hold back God's overwhelming power and make the hearing fair. Christians have often read this longing as pointing ahead to Jesus, whom they see as that go-between.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Job's words here are mainly a humble admission that no human is righteous before God or a raw, even bitter, protest that God seems unfair, and on how far the book approves of that protest.
think: When someone far more powerful holds all the cards, what would make a hearing feel fair to you?
